name: Sta. Rita Hills

climate: Seasons this mild ripen Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Syrah, Riesling and Sémillon fully without cooking off their freshness.
Chardonnay, Syrah and Sauvignon Blanc sit in their sweet spot, so the wines can show the style they are known for.
Pinot Noir is at its warm limit. It can ripen too fast, giving heavy, soft wine that has lost its freshness.
Summers are close to rainless. Vines need irrigation or deep soil that stores winter rain, but disease is rare.

soil.rock: River deposits are a mix of gravel, sand and silt. They are often fertile, so vines can grow vigorously. Shale and mudstone are fine-grained rocks that hold heat well and are moderately fertile. Sandstone is sand bound into rock. It weathers to light, sandy soil that drains freely.
soil.top: The topsoil drains well and still stores water for dry spells, so vines grow evenly. Its pH is close to neutral, so vines take up the nutrients they need easily.

land: The high ground runs about 2°F cooler than the low ground. Higher vineyards ripen later and keep more acidity, so one grape can make lighter or richer wine here depending on height.
Much of it is steep. Cold air and rain run off, so frost and waterlogging are rare and soils stay thin, keeping yields low. Steep rows are slow and costly to work, often by hand.

winkler: Early and mid-season grapes make good wine.
